items.title: COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization
items.abstract: COBRA-Skills optimizes LLM agent skills by treating it as a budgeted sequential optimization problem. It uses a contextual bandit to guide the selection of skills for evaluation, prioritizing promising or informative candidates. This approach efficiently refines the skill population using execution feedback, significantly reducing optimization costs and data requirements while achieving superior performance across diverse benchmarks.
items.figure_caption: Overview of COBRA-Skills. At each round, skills in 𝒫 t \( \mathcal{P}_{t} \) are prioritized using a neural reward predictor and LinearUCB bonus based on ℋ t − 1 \( \mathcal{H}_{t-1} \) (\( \scriptsize \)1⃝), and the highest-priority skill is evaluated by the target agent (\( \scriptsize \)2⃝). The resulting reward and trajectories update the optimization history and scoring model (\( \scriptsize \)3⃝). At scheduled population updates (performed periodically rather than after every round), new skills are evolved from accumulated evidence (\( \scriptsize \)4⃝), and the updated priority scores from \( \scriptsize \)1⃝ identify low-priority skills, which are replaced by the newly evolved skills to form 𝒫 t + 1 \( \mathcal{P}_{t+1} \) (\( \scriptsize \)5⃝). Dashed borders and arrows indicate scheduled-only operations.

items.title: Artificial Id: Drive and Persistent Alignment in Agentic AI
items.abstract: This paper introduces an "artificial id" as an internal, adaptive drive for agentic AI systems. This mechanism allows agents to autonomously decide when to continue, stop, or change their behavior, moving beyond externally defined control. The core contribution is demonstrating that such adaptive direction and persistent alignment can emerge organically through differential persistence, even in agents lacking general reasoning capabilities.
items.figure_caption: Functional architecture of the artificial id. Current language models provide the general reasoning associated here with the ego. The experiment isolates a minimal adaptive drive whose behavior is shaped through differential persistence in an environment. In the proposed coupled architecture, the id influences what the system continues to pursue, the ego translates that state into task-specific reasoning and action, and the resulting changes to the system and its environment become new input to the id. The right panel situates this loop within a persistent alignment boundary. Across the proposed architecture, that boundary comprises trusted observations, consequence channels, persistent state, authority, identity, provenance and hard constraints. Variation and differential persistence are the learning mechanism used in the experiment to produce adaptive drive; they are not required components of the proposed deployed id. The integrated architecture is proposed and is not tested here.

items.title: Autonomy, Social Norms, and Alignment: Towards a Developmental Framework for Autonomous Artificial Agents
items.abstract: This paper proposes a developmental framework for autonomous AI agents, moving beyond static datasets to enable learning through environmental interaction. Its core method involves incorporating intrinsic motivations like curiosity and competence to guide exploration, thereby enhancing autonomy. The key contribution is addressing the complex challenge of aligning these increasingly independent agents with human goals in dynamic, unstructured environments.

items.title: Domain-Specific Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
items.abstract: This paper proposes a multi-signal pipeline for detecting hallucinations in LLM-generated text, combining a fine-tuned classifier, Monte Carlo Dropout for uncertainty, and temperature scaling. The core contribution is a robust detection method that achieves high accuracy on various tasks and demonstrates genuine reasoning capabilities, not just pattern matching. Additionally, the work shows that a significant portion of performance can be achieved with limited training data and applies DPO to reduce hallucinations in a generator model.

items.title: Ecdysis: Efficient and Effective Training of Runtime Harnesses for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Ecdysis addresses the inefficiency of training LLM agent runtime harnesses by introducing principled failure diagnosis. Instead of simply iterating on observed failures, Ecdysis distinguishes between model-specific and harness-specific issues. This allows for more targeted and efficient optimization of the harness, leading to improved generalization and reduced training time.

items.title: LOCUS: Task-Aware Low-Rank Post-Training for Token-Efficient Language Generation
items.abstract: LOCUS is a task-aware, low-rank adaptation method for post-training large language models. It efficiently minimizes generation length by adapting only a small subspace of parameters, thereby reducing serving costs without sacrificing response utility. This approach achieves significant length reductions while updating a minimal fraction of the model's parameters.

items.title: MAPLE: Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution
items.abstract: MAPLE is a system that helps domain experts solve optimization problems using natural language. Its core method combines language understanding, mathematical programming, and evolutionary search to create and adapt optimization models. MAPLE's contribution is enabling rapid, iterative updates to optimization problems by remembering past decisions and search results, making optimization more accessible and adaptable to dynamic real-world scenarios.
items.figure_caption: MAPLE maintains plans through successive requests. The routing example shows problem revision, memory of earlier decisions, and reuse of search results. The tables compare capabilities and performance. An asterisk marks adapted baselines.

items.title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
items.abstract: This paper introduces MindTopo, a benchmark designed to evaluate foundation models' ability to reason about topological spatial relations, which are invariant under continuous deformation. The benchmark covers five cognitive properties (continuity, separation, order, enclosure, knots) at two levels (reasoning and planning) and contains over 11,000 instances. MindTopo's contribution is to shift the focus of foundation model evaluation from metric properties to the more fundamental topological aspects of spatial understanding.
items.figure_caption: Overview of MindTopo . Five topological properties ( continuity , separation , order , enclosure , knots ) probed at two cognitive levels: reasoning (visual QA over rendered scenes) and planning (interactive gym).

items.title: RetroThinker: Enabling Retrospective Thinking in Speech LLMs
items.abstract: RetroThinker enables streaming SpeechLLMs to improve their reasoning by dynamically revising their thought processes during inference. It achieves this through a post-training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization, allowing the model to self-verify and correct its reasoning steps on the fly. This approach aims to overcome the accuracy-latency trade-off in SpeechLLMs for complex reasoning tasks.

items.title: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
items.abstract: SIRF addresses industrial content risk control by internalizing complex platform policies directly into model weights through continued pretraining. This "spec-internalization" allows for high-precision, ultra-low-latency risk assessment without human annotation or complex rule engines. The contribution is a foundation model that significantly improves risk handling efficiency and accuracy in real-world industrial deployments.
items.figure_caption: Black (risky) Recall@P95 vs. model size, among included, logprob-available models under this deployment interface. SIRF-8B sits above all compared open-weight (4B–400B) and closed-source models at the high-precision operating point. Excluded models: Claude, Doubao and GLM, whose APIs return no token logprobs, so no confidence ranking and hence no Recall@P can be computed; this is an interface limitation, not a capability judgment. Our core attribution to spec internalization does not rely on these cross-model comparisons but on the controlled 8B same-source study in Table 1 .

items.title: Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws
items.abstract: This paper introduces Negative Self-Distillation (NSD) to improve LLM reasoning. Unlike previous methods that force imitation of correct answers, NSD trains LLMs by having them actively avoid flawed reasoning. The core idea is to use the model itself to generate "negative" examples of incorrect reasoning, thereby encouraging more robust and exploratory problem-solving.
items.figure_caption: Overview of the NSD framework. (Left) We construct a negative teacher from the same base model via self-generated negative conditioning. (Right) The student model is optimized to diverge its distribution from that of the negative teacher.

items.title: RAG-Safety-Bench: Reliable Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented LLM Safety
items.abstract: This paper introduces RAG-Safety-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the safety implications of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Large Language Models (LLMs). Its core method isolates the impact of RAG on safety by systematically controlling the retrieved documents, separating the effects of the retriever from the LLM's generation. The main contribution is providing a clear understanding of how RAG can inadvertently compromise LLM safety, even when designed for improved reliability.
items.figure_caption: The four conditions in RAG-Safety-Bench allow for detailed safety evaluation of RAG-enabled systems.

items.title: SpecGuard: Inference-Time Backdoor Detection For Free
items.abstract: SpecGuard introduces an inference-time backdoor detection method for large language models that leverages speculative decoding. By repurposing the verification step within speculative decoding, it identifies backdoors without incurring additional computational costs or making assumptions about trigger forms. This allows for efficient and stealthy backdoor detection during runtime.

items.title: ActMap: Single-Pass Uncertainty Quantification from Generation-Time Activation Maps
items.abstract: ActMap introduces a novel white-box method for single-pass uncertainty quantification in LLMs. It compresses the entire generation-time hidden-state trajectory into a compact, fixed-size tensor (ActMap) with no added computational cost. This ActMap can then be directly probed by a lightweight classifier to determine the trustworthiness of a generated answer, localizing uncertainty signals to specific regions of the model's internal computation.
items.figure_caption: The ActMap pipeline. The LLM generates its answer normally while hooks capture the per-layer, per-token hidden-state trajectory; temporal statistics, pooling, and per-channel standardization compress it into a fixed 12 × 32 × 128 12\( \times \) 32\( \times \) 128 map, from which a compact Vision Transformer classifier reads p ⁡ ( correct ) p(\( \text{correct} \)) . Channels shown: token standard deviation, temporal slope, first segment mean (real Qwen3-8B GSM8K generation).

items.title: Characterizing Job Power Elasticity for Power-Flexible AI Training
items.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of "job power elasticity" to quantify how LLM training performance degrades with reduced GPU power. The authors propose the "Power Flexibility Index (PFI)" as a metric to measure this sensitivity and enable SLA-aware power management for AI workloads. This work is crucial for making AI training power-flexible, which can alleviate data center power constraints and improve grid utilization.
items.figure_caption: LLM training jobs vary in how quickly performance degrades under power reductions. Relatively more power flexible ( — ) jobs maintain throughput despite power reductions, while relatively less flexible ( - - ) jobs quickly lose performance at lower power. We introduce the Power Flexibility Index (PFI) , a new metric for measuring power elasticity, and conduct large-scale, systematic characterization of modern LLM training jobs. We develop a model for predicting PFI online from readily available GPU telemetry, and we demonstrate how PFI-aware power allocation improves total throughput under cluster-wide GPU power constraints and realistic job mixes.

items.title: Making Alternative Data Work: Context-Augmented LLMs for Financial Forecasting
items.abstract: This paper proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to integrate alternative data for financial forecasting. The core method involves augmenting LLMs with contextual information from these diverse, often sparse, alternative data sources. The contribution is a flexible framework that overcomes the limitations of traditional methods in handling alternative data, enabling more timely and comprehensive financial predictions.

items.title: ORCH: Organizational Principles Enable Collective Intelligence in Embodied AI
items.abstract: This paper introduces ORCH, a method for organizing embodied AI agents into task-specific hierarchical structures. ORCH leverages principles from human organization theory to combine pooled and sequential interdependencies, enabling effective coordination in complex, multi-agent scenarios like wildfire response. The contribution lies in demonstrating that flexible, principle-driven organization significantly enhances collective intelligence in embodied AI, outperforming fixed structures.
items.figure_caption: Method Overall . (A) The team hierarchy was designed based on the task descriptions and available worker agents, either by a human expert or an LLM with a critic agent. (B) During execution, the manager generates the plan for its worker agents; the worker agents execute the plan and provide feedback for the manager to update the plan. (C) Pooled interdependency refers to a group of agents working concurrently and independently to achieve a goal. For instance, 3 firefighters each cut specific target trees (yellow color) to achieve the goal of cutting a group of target trees. (D) Sequential interdependency refers to a group of agents working sequentially to achieve a goal. For instance, to extinguish a fire, the firefighters must first scout the location of the fire; then the helicopter picks up and drops off the firefighters near the fire; finally, the firefighters extinguish the fire. (E) ORCH enforces hybrid collaboration mode (pooled and sequential interdependency).

items.title: Recognizing Is Not Reversing: A Controlled Inversion Test of Fact-Preserving News Framing
items.abstract: This paper introduces a novel "controlled inversion test" to assess if Large Language Models (LLMs) can reverse news framing while preserving factual accuracy. The core method involves creating paired news article variants with identical facts but different framings, then testing if LLMs can undo the framing. The key contribution is demonstrating that LLMs can recognize framing but struggle significantly to reverse it without altering facts, revealing a crucial gap between understanding and undoing framing.

items.title: When Agents Disagree: Bayesian Backward Reasoning as a Label-Free Anchor for Multi-Agent Collective Decision-Making
items.abstract: This paper proposes Bayesian backward reasoning as a novel approach for multi-agent collective decision-making, particularly when agents disagree. Instead of relying on traditional forward reasoning, it constructs a "reverse posterior" by reasoning backward from an explicit likelihood. This different factorization of information allows for a more robust assessment of agent reliability, using Jensen-Shannon divergence to rank agents based on their cross-path consistency, ultimately leading to improved collective decisions.
items.figure_caption: Reverse-anchored aggregation, left to right. Input x x is decomposed into contextual evidence a a and remaining evidence e e under the structure a → d → e a{\( \rightarrow \)}d{\( \rightarrow \)}e . The forward path (yellow) produces agent posteriors F i F_{i} , while the reverse path (blue) produces a shared reverse posterior R ∝ P ⁡ ( e ∣ d ) ​ P ​ ( d ∣ a ) R\( \propto \) P(e\( \mid \) d)\,P(d\( \mid \) a) . The shared anchor signal (green), D i = JS ⁡ ( F i , R ) D_{i}=\( \mathrm{JS} \)(F_{i},R) , guides all three heads: MinJS selects one F i F_{i} , FwdJS reweights { F i } \{F_{i}\} , and LogLin additionally incorporates R R into the output. The dashed box denotes optional labeled calibration R → R ′ R{\( \to \)}R^{\( \prime \)} . The dashed blue arrow indicates the direct contribution of R R to LogLin.

items.title: CausalArena: Benchmarking Causal Discovery in the Foundation Model Era
items.abstract: CausalArena addresses the challenge of evaluating causal discovery methods, especially with the rise of foundation models, by providing a unified and adaptable benchmark. Its core method involves a common protocol and diverse Structural Causal Models (SCMs), including synthetic, semantic, and formula-grounded types, to offer controlled breadth and human-auditable environments. The contribution is a more reliable and interpretable evaluation framework that accounts for potential biases in existing benchmarks and better assesses true causal discovery capabilities.
items.figure_caption: Figure 19: Complete observation-only pairwise win-rate matrix. Each cell reports how often the row method wins over the column method across per-SCM or per-dataset comparisons, after averaging repeated runs within the same unit. On each unit, F1 and SHD are compared separately (higher F1 wins, lower SHD wins, ties count as 0.5 0.5 ), and wins from both metrics are pooled into one rate. Methods are ordered by mean family-wise win rate, matching Figure 1 . Red cells indicate that the row method wins more often; blue cells indicate the opposite.

arxiv.title: CausalArena: Benchmarking Causal Discovery in the Foundation Model Era
arxiv.abstract: CausalArena addresses the challenge of evaluating causal discovery methods, especially with the rise of foundation models, by providing a unified and adaptable benchmark. Its core method involves a common protocol and diverse Structural Causal Models (SCMs), including synthetic, semantic, and formula-grounded types, to offer controlled breadth and human-auditable environments. The contribution is a more reliable and interpretable evaluation framework that accounts for potential biases in existing benchmarks and better assesses true causal discovery capabilities.
arxiv.figure_caption: Figure 19: Complete observation-only pairwise win-rate matrix. Each cell reports how often the row method wins over the column method across per-SCM or per-dataset comparisons, after averaging repeated runs within the same unit. On each unit, F1 and SHD are compared separately (higher F1 wins, lower SHD wins, ties count as 0.5 0.5 ), and wins from both metrics are pooled into one rate. Methods are ordered by mean family-wise win rate, matching Figure 1 . Red cells indicate that the row method wins more often; blue cells indicate the opposite.

papers.title: COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization
papers.abstract: COBRA-Skills optimizes LLM agent skills by treating it as a budgeted sequential optimization problem. It uses a contextual bandit to guide the selection of skills for evaluation, prioritizing promising or informative candidates. This approach efficiently refines the skill population using execution feedback, significantly reducing optimization costs and data requirements while achieving superior performance across diverse benchmarks.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of COBRA-Skills. At each round, skills in 𝒫 t \( \mathcal{P}_{t} \) are prioritized using a neural reward predictor and LinearUCB bonus based on ℋ t − 1 \( \mathcal{H}_{t-1} \) (\( \scriptsize \)1⃝), and the highest-priority skill is evaluated by the target agent (\( \scriptsize \)2⃝). The resulting reward and trajectories update the optimization history and scoring model (\( \scriptsize \)3⃝). At scheduled population updates (performed periodically rather than after every round), new skills are evolved from accumulated evidence (\( \scriptsize \)4⃝), and the updated priority scores from \( \scriptsize \)1⃝ identify low-priority skills, which are replaced by the newly evolved skills to form 𝒫 t + 1 \( \mathcal{P}_{t+1} \) (\( \scriptsize \)5⃝). Dashed borders and arrows indicate scheduled-only operations.

papers.title: Artificial Id: Drive and Persistent Alignment in Agentic AI
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an "artificial id" as an internal, adaptive drive for agentic AI systems. This mechanism allows agents to autonomously decide when to continue, stop, or change their behavior, moving beyond externally defined control. The core contribution is demonstrating that such adaptive direction and persistent alignment can emerge organically through differential persistence, even in agents lacking general reasoning capabilities.
papers.figure_caption: Functional architecture of the artificial id. Current language models provide the general reasoning associated here with the ego. The experiment isolates a minimal adaptive drive whose behavior is shaped through differential persistence in an environment. In the proposed coupled architecture, the id influences what the system continues to pursue, the ego translates that state into task-specific reasoning and action, and the resulting changes to the system and its environment become new input to the id. The right panel situates this loop within a persistent alignment boundary. Across the proposed architecture, that boundary comprises trusted observations, consequence channels, persistent state, authority, identity, provenance and hard constraints. Variation and differential persistence are the learning mechanism used in the experiment to produce adaptive drive; they are not required components of the proposed deployed id. The integrated architecture is proposed and is not tested here.

papers.title: Autonomy, Social Norms, and Alignment: Towards a Developmental Framework for Autonomous Artificial Agents
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a developmental framework for autonomous AI agents, moving beyond static datasets to enable learning through environmental interaction. Its core method involves incorporating intrinsic motivations like curiosity and competence to guide exploration, thereby enhancing autonomy. The key contribution is addressing the complex challenge of aligning these increasingly independent agents with human goals in dynamic, unstructured environments.

papers.title: Domain-Specific Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a multi-signal pipeline for detecting hallucinations in LLM-generated text, combining a fine-tuned classifier, Monte Carlo Dropout for uncertainty, and temperature scaling. The core contribution is a robust detection method that achieves high accuracy on various tasks and demonstrates genuine reasoning capabilities, not just pattern matching. Additionally, the work shows that a significant portion of performance can be achieved with limited training data and applies DPO to reduce hallucinations in a generator model.

papers.title: Ecdysis: Efficient and Effective Training of Runtime Harnesses for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Ecdysis addresses the inefficiency of training LLM agent runtime harnesses by introducing principled failure diagnosis. Instead of simply iterating on observed failures, Ecdysis distinguishes between model-specific and harness-specific issues. This allows for more targeted and efficient optimization of the harness, leading to improved generalization and reduced training time.

papers.title: LOCUS: Task-Aware Low-Rank Post-Training for Token-Efficient Language Generation
papers.abstract: LOCUS is a task-aware, low-rank adaptation method for post-training large language models. It efficiently minimizes generation length by adapting only a small subspace of parameters, thereby reducing serving costs without sacrificing response utility. This approach achieves significant length reductions while updating a minimal fraction of the model's parameters.

papers.title: MAPLE: Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution
papers.abstract: MAPLE is a system that helps domain experts solve optimization problems using natural language. Its core method combines language understanding, mathematical programming, and evolutionary search to create and adapt optimization models. MAPLE's contribution is enabling rapid, iterative updates to optimization problems by remembering past decisions and search results, making optimization more accessible and adaptable to dynamic real-world scenarios.
papers.figure_caption: MAPLE maintains plans through successive requests. The routing example shows problem revision, memory of earlier decisions, and reuse of search results. The tables compare capabilities and performance. An asterisk marks adapted baselines.

papers.title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MindTopo, a benchmark designed to evaluate foundation models' ability to reason about topological spatial relations, which are invariant under continuous deformation. The benchmark covers five cognitive properties (continuity, separation, order, enclosure, knots) at two levels (reasoning and planning) and contains over 11,000 instances. MindTopo's contribution is to shift the focus of foundation model evaluation from metric properties to the more fundamental topological aspects of spatial understanding.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of MindTopo . Five topological properties ( continuity , separation , order , enclosure , knots ) probed at two cognitive levels: reasoning (visual QA over rendered scenes) and planning (interactive gym).

papers.title: RetroThinker: Enabling Retrospective Thinking in Speech LLMs
papers.abstract: RetroThinker enables streaming SpeechLLMs to improve their reasoning by dynamically revising their thought processes during inference. It achieves this through a post-training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization, allowing the model to self-verify and correct its reasoning steps on the fly. This approach aims to overcome the accuracy-latency trade-off in SpeechLLMs for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
papers.abstract: SIRF addresses industrial content risk control by internalizing complex platform policies directly into model weights through continued pretraining. This "spec-internalization" allows for high-precision, ultra-low-latency risk assessment without human annotation or complex rule engines. The contribution is a foundation model that significantly improves risk handling efficiency and accuracy in real-world industrial deployments.
papers.figure_caption: Black (risky) Recall@P95 vs. model size, among included, logprob-available models under this deployment interface. SIRF-8B sits above all compared open-weight (4B–400B) and closed-source models at the high-precision operating point. Excluded models: Claude, Doubao and GLM, whose APIs return no token logprobs, so no confidence ranking and hence no Recall@P can be computed; this is an interface limitation, not a capability judgment. Our core attribution to spec internalization does not rely on these cross-model comparisons but on the controlled 8B same-source study in Table 1 .

papers.title: Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Negative Self-Distillation (NSD) to improve LLM reasoning. Unlike previous methods that force imitation of correct answers, NSD trains LLMs by having them actively avoid flawed reasoning. The core idea is to use the model itself to generate "negative" examples of incorrect reasoning, thereby encouraging more robust and exploratory problem-solving.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of the NSD framework. (Left) We construct a negative teacher from the same base model via self-generated negative conditioning. (Right) The student model is optimized to diverge its distribution from that of the negative teacher.

papers.title: RAG-Safety-Bench: Reliable Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented LLM Safety
papers.abstract: This paper introduces RAG-Safety-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the safety implications of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Large Language Models (LLMs). Its core method isolates the impact of RAG on safety by systematically controlling the retrieved documents, separating the effects of the retriever from the LLM's generation. The main contribution is providing a clear understanding of how RAG can inadvertently compromise LLM safety, even when designed for improved reliability.
papers.figure_caption: The four conditions in RAG-Safety-Bench allow for detailed safety evaluation of RAG-enabled systems.

papers.title: SpecGuard: Inference-Time Backdoor Detection For Free
papers.abstract: SpecGuard introduces an inference-time backdoor detection method for large language models that leverages speculative decoding. By repurposing the verification step within speculative decoding, it identifies backdoors without incurring additional computational costs or making assumptions about trigger forms. This allows for efficient and stealthy backdoor detection during runtime.

papers.title: ActMap: Single-Pass Uncertainty Quantification from Generation-Time Activation Maps
papers.abstract: ActMap introduces a novel white-box method for single-pass uncertainty quantification in LLMs. It compresses the entire generation-time hidden-state trajectory into a compact, fixed-size tensor (ActMap) with no added computational cost. This ActMap can then be directly probed by a lightweight classifier to determine the trustworthiness of a generated answer, localizing uncertainty signals to specific regions of the model's internal computation.
papers.figure_caption: The ActMap pipeline. The LLM generates its answer normally while hooks capture the per-layer, per-token hidden-state trajectory; temporal statistics, pooling, and per-channel standardization compress it into a fixed 12 × 32 × 128 12\( \times \) 32\( \times \) 128 map, from which a compact Vision Transformer classifier reads p ⁡ ( correct ) p(\( \text{correct} \)) . Channels shown: token standard deviation, temporal slope, first segment mean (real Qwen3-8B GSM8K generation).

papers.title: Characterizing Job Power Elasticity for Power-Flexible AI Training
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of "job power elasticity" to quantify how LLM training performance degrades with reduced GPU power. The authors propose the "Power Flexibility Index (PFI)" as a metric to measure this sensitivity and enable SLA-aware power management for AI workloads. This work is crucial for making AI training power-flexible, which can alleviate data center power constraints and improve grid utilization.
papers.figure_caption: LLM training jobs vary in how quickly performance degrades under power reductions. Relatively more power flexible ( — ) jobs maintain throughput despite power reductions, while relatively less flexible ( - - ) jobs quickly lose performance at lower power. We introduce the Power Flexibility Index (PFI) , a new metric for measuring power elasticity, and conduct large-scale, systematic characterization of modern LLM training jobs. We develop a model for predicting PFI online from readily available GPU telemetry, and we demonstrate how PFI-aware power allocation improves total throughput under cluster-wide GPU power constraints and realistic job mixes.

papers.title: Making Alternative Data Work: Context-Augmented LLMs for Financial Forecasting
papers.abstract: This paper proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to integrate alternative data for financial forecasting. The core method involves augmenting LLMs with contextual information from these diverse, often sparse, alternative data sources. The contribution is a flexible framework that overcomes the limitations of traditional methods in handling alternative data, enabling more timely and comprehensive financial predictions.

papers.title: ORCH: Organizational Principles Enable Collective Intelligence in Embodied AI
papers.abstract: This paper introduces ORCH, a method for organizing embodied AI agents into task-specific hierarchical structures. ORCH leverages principles from human organization theory to combine pooled and sequential interdependencies, enabling effective coordination in complex, multi-agent scenarios like wildfire response. The contribution lies in demonstrating that flexible, principle-driven organization significantly enhances collective intelligence in embodied AI, outperforming fixed structures.
papers.figure_caption: Method Overall . (A) The team hierarchy was designed based on the task descriptions and available worker agents, either by a human expert or an LLM with a critic agent. (B) During execution, the manager generates the plan for its worker agents; the worker agents execute the plan and provide feedback for the manager to update the plan. (C) Pooled interdependency refers to a group of agents working concurrently and independently to achieve a goal. For instance, 3 firefighters each cut specific target trees (yellow color) to achieve the goal of cutting a group of target trees. (D) Sequential interdependency refers to a group of agents working sequentially to achieve a goal. For instance, to extinguish a fire, the firefighters must first scout the location of the fire; then the helicopter picks up and drops off the firefighters near the fire; finally, the firefighters extinguish the fire. (E) ORCH enforces hybrid collaboration mode (pooled and sequential interdependency).

papers.title: Recognizing Is Not Reversing: A Controlled Inversion Test of Fact-Preserving News Framing
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel "controlled inversion test" to assess if Large Language Models (LLMs) can reverse news framing while preserving factual accuracy. The core method involves creating paired news article variants with identical facts but different framings, then testing if LLMs can undo the framing. The key contribution is demonstrating that LLMs can recognize framing but struggle significantly to reverse it without altering facts, revealing a crucial gap between understanding and undoing framing.

papers.title: When Agents Disagree: Bayesian Backward Reasoning as a Label-Free Anchor for Multi-Agent Collective Decision-Making
papers.abstract: This paper proposes Bayesian backward reasoning as a novel approach for multi-agent collective decision-making, particularly when agents disagree. Instead of relying on traditional forward reasoning, it constructs a "reverse posterior" by reasoning backward from an explicit likelihood. This different factorization of information allows for a more robust assessment of agent reliability, using Jensen-Shannon divergence to rank agents based on their cross-path consistency, ultimately leading to improved collective decisions.
